entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.1-Job.4.1">Job 36:1-4   1</reference>  Then Elihu continued and said:   2  Suffer me a little, and I will inform thee, <div eID="gen8492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> For there is something still to be said for Eloah.   3  I will fetch my knowledge from afar, <div eID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8494" type="x-p"/> And to my Creator will I ascribe right.   4  For truly my words are not lies, <div eID="gen8494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8495" type="x-p"/> One perfect in knowledge stands before thee. <div eID="gen8495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8496" type="x-p"/> Elihu’s preceding three speeches were introduced by ויּען; this fourth, in honour of the number three, is introduced only as a continuation of the others. Job is to wait yet a little while, for he still has (= עוד לּי), or: there still are, words in favour of Eloah; i.e., what may be said in vindication of God against Job’s complaints and accusations is not yet exhausted. This appears to be the only instance of the Aramaic כּתּר being taken up as Hebr.; whereas הוּה, <hi type="italic">nunciare</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">wḥâ</hi>, I, IV), is a poetic Aramaism occurring even in <reference osisRef="Ps.19.3">Psa 19:3</reference> (comp. on the construction <reference osisRef="Job.32.6">Job 32:6</reference>); and זעיר (a diminutive form, after the manner of the Arab. <hi type="italic">zu‛air</hi>) belongs in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference> to the popular language (of Jerusalem), but is here used poetically. The verb נשׂא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference></hi>, is not to be understood according to נשׂא משׁל, but according to 1Ki 10:11; and למרחוק signifies, as also <reference osisRef="Job.39.29">Job 39:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>, <hi type="italic">e longinquo,</hi> viz., out of the wide realm of history and nature. The expression נתן צדק follows the analogy of (עז) נתן כבוד. דּעה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.4">Job 36:4</reference></hi>, interchanges with the דּע which belongs exclusively to Elihu, since Elihu styles himself תּמים דּעות, as <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference> God תּמים דּעים (comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>, אל דּעות). תמים in this combination with דעות cannot be intended of purity of character; but as Elihu there attributes absolute perfection of knowledge in every direction to God, so here, in reference to the theodicy which he opposes to Job, he claims faultlessness and clearness of perception.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.5-Job.7.5">Job 36:5-7   5</reference>  Behold, God is mighty, and yet doth not act scornfully, <div eID="gen8496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8497" type="x-p"/> Mighty in power of understanding.   6  He preserveth not the life of the ungodly, <div eID="gen8497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8498" type="x-p"/> And to the afflicted He giveth right.   7  He withdraweth not His eyes from the righteous, <div eID="gen8498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8499" type="x-p"/> But with kings on the throne <div eID="gen8499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8500" type="x-p"/> He establisheth them for ever, and they are exalted. <div eID="gen8500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8501" type="x-p"/> The obj. that must be mentally supplied to ימאס ולא is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>, to be derived from the connection. The idea of the verb is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.8.20">Job 8:20</reference> : He is exalted, without however looking down disdainfully (<hi type="italic">non despicit</hi>) from His height, or more definitely: without setting Himself above the justice due to even the meanest of His creatures - great in power of heart (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.34.33">Job 34:33</reference> אנשׁי לבב, Arab. <hi type="italic">ûlû - l - elbâb</hi>), i.e., understanding (νοῦς πνεῦμα), to see through right and wrong everywhere and altogether. <reference osisRef="Job.36.6">Job 36:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">Job 36:7</reference> describe how His rule among men evinces this not merely outward but spiritual superiority coupled with condescension to the lowly. The notion of the object, ואת־מלכים לכּסּא (as <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Isa 9:11</reference> the subject), becomes the more distinctly prominent by virtue of the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> which follows like a conclusion, and takes it up again. Ewald thinks this explanation contrary to the accents and the structure of the sentence itself; but it is perfectly consistent with the former, and indisputably syntactic (Ges. §129, 2, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and Ew. himself, §344, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.132.12">Psa 132:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Isa 47:1</reference>, shows how לכסא is intended (He causes them to sit upon the throne). <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">Job 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; Psa 113:7. are parallel passages.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.8-Job.10.8">Job 36:8-10   8</reference>  And if they are bound with chains, <div eID="gen8501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8502" type="x-p"/> Holden in cords of affliction:   9  Then He declareth to them their doing <div eID="gen8502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8503" type="x-p"/> And their transgressions, that they have been vainglorious; 10  Then He openeth their ear to warning, <div eID="gen8503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8504" type="x-p"/> And commandeth them to turn from iniquity. <div eID="gen8504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8505" type="x-p"/> The subj. is in no case the רשׁעים (Hahn), but the צדיקים, or those who are as susceptible to discipline as it is needful to them, just as in Ps 107, which in general presents many instances for an extensive comparison with the speeches of Elihu. The chains, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference></hi>, are meant literally, and the bands, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference></hi>, figuratively; the Psalmist couples both in אסירי עני וברזל, Psa 107:10. The conclusion begins with <reference osisRef="Job.36.9">Job 36:9</reference>, and is repeated in another application, Job 36:10. פּעל in the sense of <hi type="italic">maleficium</hi>, as Arab. <hi type="italic">fa‛alat</hi>, recalls מעשׂה, <hi type="italic">facinus</hi>, Job 33:17. כּי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.9">Job 36:9</reference></hi>, as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference></hi>, an objective <hi type="italic">quod</hi>. It is not translated, however, <hi type="italic">quod invaluerint</hi> (Rosenm.), which is opposed to the most natural sense of the <hi type="italic">Hithpa.,</hi> but according to <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">Job 15:25</reference> : <hi type="italic">quod sese extulerint.</hi> מוּסר, παιδεία, <hi type="italic">disciplina</hi>, interchanges here with the more rare מסר used in <reference osisRef="Job.33.16">Job 33:16</reference>; there we have already also met with the phrase גּלה אזן, to uncover the ear, i.e., to open. אמר כּי corresponds to the Arab. <hi type="italic">amara an</hi> (<hi type="italic">bi - an</hi>), to command that. The fundamental thought of Elihu here once again comes unmistakeably to view: the sufferings of the righteous are well-meant chastisements, which are to wean them from the sins into which through carnal security they have fallen - a warning from God to penitence, designed to work their good.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.11-Job.12.11">Job 36:11-12 11</reference>  If they hear and yield, <div eID="gen8505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8506" type="x-p"/> They pass their days in prosperity <div eID="gen8506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8507" type="x-p"/> And their years in pleasure. 12  And if they hear not, <div eID="gen8507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8508" type="x-p"/> They pass away by the bow <div eID="gen8508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> And expire in lack of knowledge. <div eID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> Since a declaration of the divine will has preceded in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference></hi>, it is more natural to take ויעבדוּ in the sense of <hi type="italic">obsequi</hi>, to do the will of another (as 1Ki 12:7, comp. מעבּד from עבד in the generalized sense of <hi type="italic">facere</hi>), than, with Umbr., in the sense of <hi type="italic">colere scil. Deum</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">Isa 19:23</reference>, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛âbid</hi>, one who reveres God, a godly person). Instead of יבלּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.22">Isa 65:22</reference> (on which the Masora observes לית, i.e., “nowhere else”) and <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job 21:13</reference> <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, 'it is here without dispute יכלּוּ (Targ. ישׁלּמוּן, <hi type="italic">peragent</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.27">Eze 43:27</reference>). נעימים is, as <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, a neutral masc.: <hi type="italic">amoena</hi>. Impenitence changes affliction, which is intended to be a means of rescue, into total destruction; yet there are some who will not be warned and affrighted by it.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.13-Job.15.13">Job 36:13-15 13</reference>  Yet the hypocrites in heart cherish wrath, <div eID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> They cry not when He hath chained them. 14  Thus their soul dieth in the vigour of youth, <div eID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> And their life is like that of the unclean. 15  Yet He delivereth the sufferer by his affliction, <div eID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> And openeth their ear by oppression. <div eID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8514" type="x-p"/> He who is angry with God in his affliction, and does not humbly pray to Him, shows thereby that he is a חנף, one estranged from God (on the idea of the root, vid., i. 216), and not a צדיק. This connection renders it natural to understand not the divine wrath by אף: θησαυρίζουσιν ὀργήν (Rosenm. after <reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Rom 2:5</reference>), or: they heap up wrath upon themselves (Wolfson, who supplies עליהם), but the impatience, discontent, and murmuring of man himself: they cherish or harbour wrath, viz., בּלבּם (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.22.22">Job 22:22</reference>, where שׁים בלב signifies to take to heart, but at the same time to preserve in the heart). Used thus absolutely, שׂים signifies elsewhere in the book, to give attention to, <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>, or (as Arab. <hi type="italic">wḍ‛</hi>) to lay down a pledge; here it signifies <hi type="italic">reponunt s. recondunt</hi> (with an implied <hi type="italic">in ipsis</hi>), as also Arab. <hi type="italic">šâm , fut. i,</hi> to conceal with the idea of sinking into (<hi type="italic">immittentem</hi>), e.g., the sword in the sheath. With תּמת, for ותּמת (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference>) or ותמת, the punishment which issues forth undistinguished from this frustration of the divine purpose of grace follows ἀσυνδέτως, as e.g., Hos 7:16. חיּה interchanges with נפשׁ, as <reference osisRef="Job.33.22">Job 33:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">Job 33:28</reference>; נער (likewise a favourite word with Elihu) is intended just as <reference osisRef="Job.33.25">Job 33:25</reference>, and in the <reference osisRef="Ps.88.16">Psa 88:16</reference>, which resembles both the Elihu section and the rest of the book. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּקּדשׁים has the sense of <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi> (Targ. היך), as <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>, comp. תּחת, Job 34:26. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.36.19-Job.21.19">Job 36:19-21 19</reference>  Shall thy crying place thee beyond distress, <div eID="gen8520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8521" type="x-p"/> And all the efforts of strength? 20  Long not for the night to come, <div eID="gen8521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> Which shall remove people from their place! 21  Take heed, incline not to evil; <div eID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> For this thou hast desired more than affliction. <div eID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8524" type="x-p"/> Those expositors who found in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference></hi> the warning, that Job should not imagine that he would be able to redeem himself from judgment by a large ransom, go on to explain: will He esteem thy riches? (Farisol, Rosenm., Umbr., Carey, Ebr., and others); or: will thy riches suffice? (Hirz., Schlottm.); or some other way (Ew.). But apart from the want of connection of this insinuation, which is otherwise not mentioned in the book, and apart from the violence which must be done to היערך to accommodate it to it, שׁוּע, although it might, as the abstract of שׁוע, <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job 34:19</reference>, signify wealth (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">sa‛at , amplitudo</hi>), is, however, according to the usage of the language (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.30.24">Job 30:24</reference>), so far as we can trace it, a secondary form of שׁוע (שׁועה), a cry for help; and Job 35:9., <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">Job 36:13</reference>, and other passages, also point to this signification. What follows is still less appropriate to this thought of ransom; Hirz. translates: Oh, not God and all the treasures of wealth! But בּצר is nowhere equivalent to בּצר, <reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference>; but צר, <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>, signifies distress; and the expression לא בצר, in a condition devoid of distress, is like לא בחכמה, <reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>, and לא ביד, Job 34:20.
